theme: The feasts of the LORD; the lampstand and bread
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 23:1-24:23. Chapter 23 lays out the yearly calendar of Israel’s festivals. Read it as a map of the year, and watch how often the word “rest” and the word “holy” appear.
settingTheScene: The festivals of Israel mark the rhythm of the year around the agricultural seasons and, more importantly, around the great acts of God. They begin with the weekly Sabbath and run through Passover, Unleavened Bread, First Fruits, Weeks, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Booths. Chapter 24 returns to the tabernacle with the lamp and the bread, and then describes an incident of blasphemy that leads to a ruling about justice. The chapters show that holiness extends to time as well as to space.
observation: “These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at their appointed times” (23:2).
The weekly Sabbath comes first in the list (23:3).
The Passover is on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by the seven days of Unleavened Bread (23:4-8).
The first sheaf of the harvest is waved before the LORD as First Fruits (23:9-14).
The Feast of Weeks comes fifty days after First Fruits, with a new grain offering (23:15-22).
The Feast of Trumpets and the Day of Atonement are in the seventh month (23:23-32).

The Feast of Booths lasts a week, and the people live in booths “that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (23:33-43).
A man who blasphemes the name is stoned, and the principle is stated: “You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native” (24:10-23).
interpretation:
The calendar in Leviticus 23 makes a point that is easy to miss: time itself belongs to God. Israel’s year was not a series of random days. It was a story told in seasons. Passover recalled the night of the exodus. First Fruits recognized that the harvest belonged to the LORD. Weeks gave thanks for the grain. Trumpets and the Day of Atonement called the people to repentance. Booths celebrated God’s provision in the wilderness. Every year, the people were reminded of who God is and what he has done.

The list begins with the Sabbath. Before the great festivals, there is the weekly rhythm of rest. The seventh day, each week, is a “holy convocation.” It was the oldest feast, established at creation, and the foundation of the others. The point is that Israel’s whole life is a pattern of work and rest, of effort and gratitude.

Notice how each festival is a response to something God did. They are not mainly about human achievement. Passover remembers rescue. Booths remembers the wilderness. First Fruits acknowledges that the harvest is a gift. The festivals teach the people to remember, and remembering is one of the main commands of the Old Testament. They are a form of teaching, put into the shape of a year.

The festivals also look forward. The harvest festivals point to a greater ingathering. The Day of Atonement points to a final cleansing. The feast of Booths, with its joy and its prospect of rest in the land, points to the day when God will live with his people forever.

The last part of chapter 24 includes the case of a man who cursed God’s name. The point is that the name of the LORD is not to be treated lightly, and that the same law applies to everyone, native or sojourner. Justice does not play favorites.
connection: The New Testament sees the festivals fulfilled in Christ. He is the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). He is the “firstfruits” of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20). The Spirit came at Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks (Acts 2:1-4). Jesus stood in the temple at the Feast of Booths and said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). Colossians 2:16-17 calls the festivals “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” The church celebrates the Lord’s Day as a weekly remembrance of the resurrection.
application:
Think about your own calendar. Does it reflect what God has done, or does it only reflect your work?

Choose one rhythm this year, such as a weekly day of rest, or an annual time to remember God’s faithfulness, and plan for it.

Thank God for the way each of the festivals points to Christ.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to number your days.
Thank him for Jesus, the Passover lamb and the firstfruits.
Ask him to let the rhythm of your life be shaped by his goodness.
